_comment: Nutrient interaction matrix for FeedForward's bioavailability engine. Each entry is a documented mechanism by which one dietary factor changes the absorption (or, where noted, the retention) of a nutrient. 'factor' is the multiplicative effect when the modifier co-occurs in a meal (>1 enhances, <1 inhibits). Magnitudes are mid-range values from the cited literature and are deliberately conservative. Several mineral-mineral competitions are most pronounced at high/supplemental doses; these are marked in the mechanism and given mild factors. CITATIONS ARE REPRESENTATIVE ANCHORS AND MUST BE VERIFIED AGAINST SOURCE BEFORE ANY CLINICAL USE. See docs/SCIENTIFIC_BASIS.md.

_schema.target: nutrient whose absorption is affected (nutrient id, or form: heme_iron/non_heme_iron/beta_carotene)
_schema.evidence: A-D grade for the interaction itself
_schema.dose_note: optional: context in which the interaction is most relevant

interactions.mechanism: Ascorbic acid reduces ferric (Fe3+) to absorbable ferrous (Fe2+) iron and forms a soluble chelate.
The 'meat factor' (MFP) from muscle tissue enhances non-heme iron uptake.
Vitamin A and beta-carotene form soluble complexes with iron, keeping it available and counteracting phytate inhibition.
Fructose and other organic sugars chelate iron into a more absorbable form.
interactions.dose_note: No verified citation is attached; the factor is a conservative placeholder, not a measured coefficient.

interactions.mechanism: Citric, malic and lactic acids solubilise non-heme iron, improving uptake.
Phytic acid binds iron in the gut lumen forming an insoluble, unabsorbable complex.
Polyphenols/tannins (tea, coffee) form insoluble complexes with non-heme iron.
Calcium competes with iron at the enterocyte, reducing iron uptake when co-ingested.
Some dietary fibres bind non-heme iron, modestly reducing absorption.
Oxalate can bind non-heme iron, modestly lowering its availability.
Vitamin D upregulates intestinal calcium-binding proteins, increasing active absorption.
Oxalic acid binds calcium into insoluble calcium oxalate (e.g. spinach ~5% absorbed).
Phytate chelates calcium, modestly reducing its absorption.
Caffeine slightly increases urinary calcium loss, marginally reducing net retention.
interactions.dose_note: small effect, offset by adequate intake

interactions.mechanism: High sodium intake increases urinary calcium excretion, reducing retention.
Animal protein counteracts phytate inhibition and provides absorption-promoting amino acids.
Phytate is the primary dietary inhibitor of zinc absorption, forming insoluble complexes.
High calcium can modestly reduce zinc absorption, particularly with phytate present.
A high iron-to-zinc ratio competes for shared uptake pathways.
Some fibres bind zinc, modestly lowering absorption.
Phytate binds magnesium, reducing its bioavailability from high-phytate foods.
High fibre intake can modestly reduce magnesium absorption.
High zinc induces intestinal metallothionein, which binds copper and blocks its absorption.
interactions.dose_note: clinically important at high zinc intakes

interactions.mechanism: Very high vitamin C intake can impair copper absorption/status.
Phytate binds manganese, reducing absorption from high-phytate plant foods.
Iron and manganese share absorption pathways and compete when iron is high.
interactions.dose_note: No verified citation is attached; the factor is a conservative placeholder, not a measured coefficient.

interactions.mechanism: High calcium modestly reduces manganese absorption.
interactions.dose_note: No verified citation is attached; the factor is a conservative placeholder, not a measured coefficient.

interactions.mechanism: Vitamin C protects natural folate from oxidative degradation, preserving availability.
Preformed vitamin A and provitamin carotenoids require dietary fat for micellar absorption.
Vitamin D is fat-soluble; dietary fat improves its intestinal absorption.
Magnesium is a cofactor for the enzymes that activate vitamin D, supporting its function.
Tocopherols require dietary fat and bile for micelle formation and uptake.
Vitamin K absorption is fat-dependent and enhanced when consumed with lipids.
Carotenoid absorption rises several-fold with even modest dietary fat.
Single-meal human studies found calcium reduced absorption of both heme and non-heme iron.
interactions.dose_note: Factor matches the existing non-heme calcium multiplier. It is a conservative meal-level factor, not a coefficient fitted from the cited study.

interactions.mechanism: Alcohol interferes with folate absorption and increases urinary folate loss.
interactions.dose_note: Most relevant at higher intakes. The factor is a conservative model multiplier, not a measured coefficient from the cited review.

food_properties._comment: Keyword heuristics used to detect anti-nutrient / enhancer properties in foods at ingest time. Production would use structured composition data (e.g. USDA phytate tables); these keyword sets are a transparent approximation. Nutrient-based modifiers (fat, calcium, iron, fiber, sodium) are detected numerically at meal time, not from keywords.
